vision_assessment.summary: Against an unapproved draft of the vision: the title screen and the HUD deliver the place and the patrol identity clearly, and Koda is a first-class control from the first frame. But the first playable frames captured are indoors under an overhead camera, so 'the mountain is the world' is sold on the title screen and not yet in play, and from that camera Koda's defining look does not read. Avalanche control and rescue (pillar 2) and travel across the valley (pillar 4) were not reached by the automated session and remain unassessed.

delivers.assessment: The phone title screen shows the log station under snow-covered peaks, the patrol badge and the line 'The Kessel valley is yours to look after': Colorado high country and a working patrol, at a glance.
Koda is at Vince's heel in the first playable frame, and Bark, Stay and Pet Koda are permanent buttons on phone and desktop.
The day opens with a dispatch on the radio log ('Forty centimetres up high overnight. There is a call on your mission table.') and a distance marker to the mission table.

gaps.assessment: Every play frame captured after Start is the lodge interior from straight above: floorboards, beam shadows and a rug. The peaks that sell the title screen are not in view once control begins.
From the overhead play camera Koda reads as a grey capsule; the husky markings and the one ear that never stands up are not visible.

opportunities.title: Hand over control with the mountain in view
opportunities.observation: The title screen shows the valley; the first playable frames on phone and desktop show only the lodge floor from overhead, with heavy beam shadows across most of the screen.
opportunities.why_it_matters: The first minute of control is where the promise either lands or does not. Right now the strongest image of the place is the one the player cannot act in.
opportunities.recommendation: Start day one on the lodge porch facing Kessel Bowl with the dispatch on the radio and the mission table one step inside, or ease the camera from the title view down to Vince before handing over control. Keep the roof-lift interior for every later morning.
opportunities.expected_improvement: The player's first controllable view matches the title screen's promise. Check: the first play frame shows sky and ridge line; time from Start to first outdoor frame drops.

opportunities.title: Make Koda recognisable from the play camera
opportunities.observation: At the default overhead distance Koda is a grey elongated shape; the white mask, the curled tail and the dropped ear named in the README do not read.
opportunities.why_it_matters: Koda is one of the four pillars and the game's most personal element. A companion the player cannot recognise at a glance is harder to bond with, which is the bond the progression rewards.
opportunities.recommendation: Give Koda a top-down silhouette: contrasting white mask and chest, a curled tail, and the one dropped ear exaggerated so it reads from above; consider a slightly lower camera pitch when Vince stands still near Koda.
opportunities.expected_improvement: Koda reads as a husky in an overhead frame. Check: in a still from the play camera, people name the animal and spot the ear.

opportunities.title: Proposal: one shared mountain a day
opportunities.observation: The README says each morning's snowpack is new and seeded by the day; the game is single-player with no way to compare a day with anyone.
opportunities.playtest: Give five players the same seeded day for a week; count how many come back the next day and whether they talk about the same slide.
opportunities.why_it_matters: The daily seeded avalanche day already exists in the design. Making it the same day for every player turns the forecast into a shared event, a reason to return that comes from the game itself rather than a bolted-on reward.
opportunities.recommendation: Expose the day seed: everyone plays the same forecast and calls; at the bunk, show zones controlled, natural releases and people found, and a share card for the day.
opportunities.expected_improvement: A daily return reason built on the existing avalanche system, if the playtest shows people want to compare days.

opportunities.title: The move/look hint runs into the Stay button on iPhone
opportunities.observation: On the phone play frame the text 'Drag on the right to look' ends under the Stay button.
opportunities.why_it_matters: It is the one instruction a new player needs, on the device the game is built for.
opportunities.recommendation: Lift the hint above the button row, or fade it out after the first drag on each side.
opportunities.expected_improvement: The hint is fully readable and clears itself once learned.

opportunities.title: A 'READY' label shows under the compass on desktop
opportunities.observation: On the desktop frame right after Start, the word READY is partly hidden behind the compass strip at the top centre.
opportunities.why_it_matters: A clipped label at the top centre is the first HUD detail a desktop player sees.
opportunities.recommendation: Hide the READY label once the compass appears, or give it its own row.
opportunities.expected_improvement: A clean top bar on the first frame.

strengths.title: The title screen sells the place
strengths.observation: A rendered lodge under snow peaks, the patrol badge, KESSEL VALLEY and one warm sentence listing the station, the sled, the borrowed helicopter, the old skis and Koda.
strengths.why_it_works: It states the fantasy (you look after this valley) and the toolkit in one screen, in the game's own voice, with a single clear action.
strengths.protect: Keep it the first thing a phone shows; do not cover it with menus or sign-in.

strengths.title: A field-notebook HUD
strengths.observation: Graph-paper panels for time, temperature, danger and funds, a typewriter DISPATCH log and a compass strip, consistent on phone and desktop.
strengths.why_it_works: The interface looks like patrol paperwork rather than a generic game HUD, so even the numbers carry the identity.
strengths.protect: Keep new HUD elements in the same paper-and-typewriter language.

strengths.title: Koda has buttons of their own
strengths.observation: Bark, Stay and Pet Koda are always on screen, beside movement.
strengths.why_it_works: Making the companion a permanent control, not a menu item, delivers pillar 3 in the interface itself.
strengths.protect: Do not fold these into a menu to save space.

strengths.title: Assists are real and opt-in
strengths.observation: The pause menu offers helicopter hover and landing, sled hill hold and a route line, each explained and off by default, plus a vibration toggle.
strengths.why_it_works: Players who need help can get it without the default game being softened.
strengths.protect: Keep them explained in one line each and off by default.

observed.claim: Every probe input changed the screen (dead time 0.0); the best touch response was 295 ms and the median 636 ms, measured on software WebGL at 2.6 to 6 fps, so responsiveness on a real phone is not measured.
The pause menu shows three opt-in assists and a vibration setting, so PLAYCRAFT's 'assist or difficulty options not found in source' and 'haptics not found in source' do not hold for this build.
The automated session stayed in the lodge for the whole run: every play frame on both devices is the interior, so traversal, avalanche control and rescue were not exercised.

source_based.claim: DESIGNCRAFT's 'the player decides how fast, never what or how' reads only mission data. The README describes free patrol, four ways to travel, tricks and a seeded daily snowpack, so the player's 'how' lives in traversal and avalanche work that mission data does not describe.
PLAYCRAFT scored this build against a physics-puzzle criterion ('Skill shots are recognised'), which does not fit a patrol simulation; its genre mix pulled in a criterion the game does not aim for.

hypotheses.claim: Whether the rescue procedure (signal, coarse and fine search, probe, dig) stays tense and rewarding on the third rescue or becomes tedious.
hypotheses.playtest: Five players each do three rescue drills; note hesitations, time per phase, and whether they choose a fourth.

hypotheses.claim: Whether starting indoors and walking to the mission table delays the mountain long enough to lose a first-time player.
hypotheses.playtest: Time from Start to the first outdoor moment for five new players, and ask after two minutes what they think the game is about.

hypotheses.claim: Whether the snowmobile's weight and the ski carving feel as described in the README on a phone GPU.
hypotheses.playtest: Play on an iPhone for ten minutes of free patrol; record frame rate and ask players to describe the sled in three words.

evidence.title: The player decides how fast, never what or how
